nodes.label: Set and interval notation
nodes.description: Convert between interval notation and set notation for an interval of real numbers, using round and square brackets correctly.

nodes.label: Evaluate with function notation
nodes.description: Evaluate a function written in function notation for a given input, including sums and compositions of functions, and determine the input that gives a given output.

nodes.label: Represent functions as tables and graphs
nodes.description: Complete a table of values, plot ordered pairs, and create a table of values from a function in order to plot its graph.

nodes.label: Domain and range from graphs
nodes.description: Read values, the domain and the range from the graph of a function in context, and state what the domain and range represent.

nodes.label: Plot line, domain and range
nodes.description: Complete a table of values for a straight line function, plot the points and join them to draw the graph, and state its domain and range.

nodes.label: Gradient, y-intercept and equation
nodes.description: Write the equation of a straight line in standard form $y=mx+c$, state its gradient ($m$) and $y$-intercept ($c$) from the equation or from the graph, and give or match the equation of a line from its graph.

nodes.label: Intercepts and dual intercept method
nodes.description: Calculate the $x$-intercept and the $y$-intercept of a straight line from its equation, state whether the graph is increasing or decreasing, and sketch the graph using the dual intercept method.

nodes.label: Sketch by gradient-intercept method
nodes.description: Sketch a straight line graph using the gradient-intercept method: plot the $y$-intercept and use the gradient (change in $y$ over change in $x$) to find a second point.

nodes.label: Effects of a and q; find a and q
nodes.description: Determine the equation y=ax^2+q of a parabola from its graph, using the effect of a on the shape and the effect of q as a vertical shift, and calculate the values of a and q.

nodes.label: Domain, range, turning point
nodes.description: Determine the domain and range of a parabola y=ax^2+q, and state its turning point, axis of symmetry and where it increases or decreases.

nodes.label: Calculate parabola intercepts
nodes.description: Calculate the y-intercept and the x-intercepts of a parabola y=ax^2+q by setting x=0 and y=0, and recognise when there are no x-intercepts.

nodes.label: Sketch a parabola
nodes.description: Sketch the graph of a parabola y=ax^2+q, by plotting points or by using the sign of a, the intercepts and the turning point, and mark these on the graph.

nodes.label: Plot hyperbolas from tables
nodes.description: Complete a table of values for a hyperbola $y=\frac{a}{x}$, plot the points and join them with two smooth curves, calculate a $y$-value for a given $x$-value, and use the graph to describe its discontinuity, asymptotes and lines of symmetry.

nodes.label: Effects of a and q
nodes.description: Describe the effect of $a$ (its sign and size) and of $q$ (a vertical shift) on the graph of $y=\frac{a}{x}+q$, and identify the function that matches a given graph or describe the transformation between two hyperbolic functions.

nodes.label: Intercepts, domain and range
nodes.description: Calculate the $x$-intercept and $y$-intercept of a hyperbola from its equation, and determine its domain and range.

nodes.label: Sketch hyperbolic graphs
nodes.description: Sketch the graph of a hyperbola $y=\frac{a}{x}+q$ by finding the sign of $a$, the intercepts and the asymptotes, and mark these on the graph.

nodes.label: Find a and q from graph
nodes.description: Calculate the values of $a$ and $q$ in the standard form $y=\frac{a}{x}+q$ of a hyperbola from its graph and a point given on it.

nodes.label: Plot exponential graphs
nodes.description: Complete a table of values and draw the graphs of exponential functions of the form y = b^x (b > 0, b ≠ 1) for different values of b on the same system of axes, and describe how the graphs compare (common y-intercept, asymptote, and that (1/b)^x is the reflection of b^x in the y-axis), including how the value of b changes the graph.

nodes.label: Determine equation from graph
nodes.description: Determine the values of a and q (or the equation) of an exponential function y = ab^x + q from points on its graph, using the effects of a and q (sign of a, vertical shift), and write the equation of its reflection, vertical shift or vertical stretch.

nodes.label: Domain and range
nodes.description: Determine the domain and range of an exponential function y = ab^x + q, using the sign of a and the value of q to decide whether the range lies above or below y = q.

nodes.label: Calculate intercepts
nodes.description: Calculate the y-intercept (let x = 0) and the x-intercept (let y = 0) of an exponential function y = ab^x + q, rounding where required, and recognise when there is no x-intercept.

nodes.label: Sketch exponential graphs
nodes.description: Sketch the graph of an exponential function y = ab^x + q by examining the sign of a and the value of q and finding the intercepts and the horizontal asymptote y = q, and identify the graph that matches a given equation.

nodes.label: Plot the basic sine graph
nodes.description: Plot the graph of y = sin θ for 0° ≤ θ ≤ 360° by completing a table of values with a calculator and joining the points with a smooth curve.

nodes.label: Sketch y = a sin θ + q
nodes.description: Describe the effects of a (vertical stretch or contraction, amplitude, reflection about the x-axis) and q (vertical shift) on the graph of y = a sin θ + q, match an equation to its graph, and sketch the graph by starting from the basic sine graph and applying those effects.

nodes.label: Characteristics of sine graph
nodes.description: Determine the domain, range, period, amplitude, intercepts and turning points of a sine graph of the form f(θ) = a sin θ + q.

nodes.label: Find a and q from graph
nodes.description: Determine the values of a and q (and so the equation) of a sine graph y = a sin θ + q from points and features shown on its graph.

nodes.label: Plot cosine graph and state its characteristics
nodes.description: Plot the graph of y = cos θ for 0° ≤ θ ≤ 360° from a table of values (completed with a calculator, points joined with a smooth curve), and state the domain, range, period, amplitude, intercepts and turning points of a cosine function f(θ) = a cos θ + q.

nodes.label: Sketch y = a cos θ + q
nodes.description: Sketch the graph of y = a cos θ + q for θ ∈ [0°, 360°] without a table of values, by using the effects of a (amplitude, vertical stretch, reflection about the x-axis) and q (vertical shift).

nodes.label: Find a and q from a cosine graph
nodes.description: Determine the values of a and q in y = a cos θ + q from two points given on its graph, using the y-intercept (0°, a + q) and the range.

nodes.label: Compare the sine and cosine graphs
nodes.description: Compare the graphs of sine and cosine on the same set of axes, and express each as a horizontal shift of the other (sin θ = cos(θ − 90°), cos θ = sin(θ + 90°)).

nodes.label: Plot the tangent graph
nodes.description: Plot the graph of $y=\tan\theta$ for $0^{\circ}\le\theta\le360^{\circ}$ by using a calculator to complete a table of values and joining the plotted points with a smooth curve, marking where $\tan\theta$ is undefined.

nodes.label: Sketch a tan θ + q
nodes.description: Sketch the graph of $y=a\tan\theta+q$ for $\theta\in[0^\circ, 360^\circ]$ by using the effect of $q$ (a vertical shift) and the effect of $a$ (the steepness of the branches).

nodes.label: Tangent graph characteristics
nodes.description: State the domain, range, period, intercepts and asymptotes of a tangent graph of the form $y=a\tan\theta+q$.

nodes.label: Find a and q from graph
nodes.description: Determine the values of $a$ and $q$ in $y=a\tan\theta+q$ from two labelled points on the graph, using the $y$-intercept $(0^\circ, q)$.

nodes.label: Determine equations from graphs
nodes.description: Determine the equation of a parabola, hyperbola, exponential or trigonometric function from its graph by substituting the given points into the general form and solving for $a$ and $q$.

nodes.label: Intercepts and intersection points
nodes.description: Calculate the coordinates of the intercepts and of the points of intersection of two graphs (by letting $x=0$ or $y=0$, and by equating the two expressions), and use them to find distances and to plot functions on the same set of axes.

nodes.label: Range of trigonometric functions
nodes.description: Determine the range of a trigonometric function of the form $y=a\sin\theta+q$ or $y=a\cos\theta+q$ from its equation.

claims.claim: In set notation, {x : x ∈ R, x > 0} is read as the set of all x-values such that x is an element of the set of real numbers and is greater than 0.
In set notation, {y : y ∈ N, 3 < y ≤ 5} is read as the set of all y-values such that y is a natural number, is greater than 3 and is less than or equal to 5.
In set notation, {z : z ∈ Z, z ≤ 100} is read as the set of all z-values such that z is an integer and is less than or equal to 100.
Interval notation can only be used to represent an interval of real numbers.
In interval notation the two endpoints are written inside brackets and separated by a semicolon, for example (3, 11).
In interval notation, a round bracket indicates that the number is not included in the interval.
In interval notation, a square bracket indicates that the number is included in the interval.
In interval notation, round brackets are always used for positive and negative infinity.
The interval (3, 11) includes all real numbers greater than but not equal to 3 and less than but not equal to 11.
The interval (-∞, -2) includes all real numbers less than, but not equal to, -2.
The interval [1, 9) includes all real numbers greater than or equal to 1 and less than but not equal to 9.
A function is a mathematical relationship between two variables, where every input variable has one output variable.
Functions can take input from many variables, but always give the same output, unique to that function.
In functions, the x-variable is known as the input or independent variable, because its value can be chosen freely.
The calculated y-variable is known as the output or dependent variable, because its value depends on the chosen input value.
Function notation is another way of writing a function: y = 2x + 1 can be written as f(x) = 2x + 1.
f(x) = 2x + 1 is said as 'f of x is equal to 2x + 1'.
Any letter can be used to name a function in function notation, for example g(x), h(x) or p(x).
'Find the value of the function for x = -3' can be written as 'find f(-3)'.
To determine the output value for a given input, such as f(-3) for f(x) = 2x + 1, replace x with the input value (here -3) and calculate.
For f(x) = 2x + 1, f(-3) = -5 means that when x = -3 the value of the function is -5.
'Find the value of x that will give a y-value of 27' can be written as 'find x if f(x) = 27'.
To determine the input value that gives a given output, write the equation f(x) = output (here 2x + 1 = 27) and solve for x, which gives x = 13.
For f(x) = 2x + 1, x = 13 means that when x = 13 the value of the function is 27.
A function can be represented in words, for example: the relationship between two variables is such that one is always 5 less than the other.
A function can be represented as an algebraic formula, for example f(x) = x - 5.
A function can be represented by a mapping diagram.
Functions can be expressed in many different ways for different purposes.
A table of values lists the input variable (x) values in one row and the matching output variable (y) values in another, for example x = -3, 0, 5 with y = -8, -5, 0.
A function can be represented as a set of ordered number pairs, for example (-3, -8), (0, -5), (5, 0).
A function can be represented as a graph.
The domain of a function is the set of all independent x-values from which the function produces a single y-value for each x-value.
The range is the set of all dependent y-values which can be obtained using an independent x-value.
Graphs allow relationships to be visualised and are much easier to read and interpret than lists of numbers.
When the graphs of two people's locations as functions of time are plotted, the place where the lines cross means that the two people meet each other at that time.
Functions of the form y = mx + c are called straight line functions.
In y = mx + c, m and c are constants, and they have different effects on the graph of the function.
The standard form of a straight line graph is the equation y = mx + c.
m is referred to as the gradient of a straight-line graph.
As m increases, the gradient of the graph increases.
c is known as the y-intercept.
The value of c affects where the graph cuts the y-axis.
If c > 0, the graph shifts vertically upwards.
If c < 0, the graph shifts vertically downwards.
To complete a table of values for a function, substitute each given value of x into the equation to find the corresponding f(x).
Each pair (x, f(x)) from the table gives a point to plot, and points are written with a semicolon between the coordinates, for example (-2, -2) and (0, 0).
Plot the points from the table and join them with a straight line to draw the graph.
The domain of a straight line function is all real numbers, {x : x in R}, because there is no value of x for which f(x) is undefined.
The range of f(x) = mx + c is all real numbers, because f(x) can take on any real value.
If m > 0, the graph increases from left to right (the graph slopes upwards).
If m < 0, the graph slopes downwards.
After plotting the graph, check that the graph increases if m > 0 and that it decreases if m < 0.
Always write the function in the form y = mx + c and take note of m before sketching.
Every point on the y-axis has an x-coordinate of 0.
To calculate the y-intercept, let x = 0.
Every point on the x-axis has a y-coordinate of 0.
To calculate the x-intercept, let y = 0.
For g(x) = x - 1, letting x = 0 gives g(0) = -1, so the y-intercept is the point (0, -1).
For g(x) = x - 1, letting y = 0 gives x = 1, so the x-intercept is the point (1, 0).
To sketch a graph of the form f(x) = mx + c, three characteristics must be determined.
The three characteristics needed to sketch f(x) = mx + c are the sign of m, the y-intercept and the x-intercept.
Only two points are needed to plot a straight line graph.
In the dual intercept method, the two points used are the x-intercept and the y-intercept, as these are the easiest points to use.
Dual intercept method, step 1: examine the standard form of the equation to find the sign of m, which tells whether the graph increases or decreases.
Dual intercept method, step 2: calculate the intercepts, letting x = 0 for the y-intercept and y = 0 for the x-intercept.
Dual intercept method, step 3: plot the two intercept points and draw the graph.
A straight line graph y = mx + c can be drawn using the gradient (m) and the y-intercept (c).
In the gradient-intercept method, calculate the y-intercept by letting x = 0; this gives the first point (0, c).
In the gradient-intercept method, the gradient is used to calculate the second point.
The gradient of a line is the measure of steepness.
Steepness is determined by the ratio of vertical change to horizontal change.
The gradient m equals the change in y divided by the change in x, that is, the vertical change over the horizontal change.
The same gradient can be written as a change up and to the right, or as the matching change down and to the left; for example 3 up over 2 right equals 3 down over 2 left.
Gradient-intercept method, step 1: use the intercept. For p(x) = (1/2)x - 3, c = -3, which gives the point (0, -3).
Gradient-intercept method, step 2: use the gradient. For m = 1/2, start at (0, -3) and move 1 unit up and 2 units to the right to get the second point (2, -2).
Alternatively, from (0, -3) move 1 unit down and 2 units to the left to get the second point (-2, -4).
Gradient-intercept method, step 3: plot the two points and draw the graph.
Functions of the general form y = ax^2 + q are called parabolic functions.
In the equation y = ax^2 + q, a and q are constants, and they have different effects on the parabola.
To deduce the effect of q, complete a table of values for y = x^2 - 2, y = x^2 - 1, y = x^2, y = x^2 + 1 and y = x^2 + 2 (for x = -2, -1, 0, 1, 2) and plot the graphs on the same system of axes.
To deduce the effect of a, complete a table of values for y = -2x^2, y = -x^2, y = x^2 and y = 2x^2 (for x = -2, -1, 0, 1, 2) and plot the graphs on the same system of axes.
The effect of q is called a vertical shift: all points are moved the same distance in the same direction, so the entire graph slides up or down.
For q > 0, the graph of f(x) is shifted vertically upwards by q units.
For q < 0, the graph of f(x) is shifted vertically downwards by q units.
The sign of a determines the shape of the graph.
For a > 0, the graph of f(x) is a “smile”.
For a > 0, the graph of f(x) is stretched vertically upwards; as a gets larger, the graph gets narrower.
For 0 < a < 1, as a gets closer to 0, the graph of f(x) gets wider.
For a < 0, the graph of f(x) is a “frown”.
For a < 0, the graph of f(x) is stretched vertically downwards; as a gets smaller, the graph gets narrower.
For -1 < a < 0, as a gets closer to 0, the graph of f(x) gets wider.
The standard form of the equation of a parabola is y = ax^2 + q.
The domain of f(x) = ax^2 + q is {x : x in R} (all real numbers) because there is no value for which f(x) is undefined.
To find the range when a > 0, start from x^2 >= 0 (a perfect square is always positive).
Since a > 0, multiplying x^2 >= 0 by a gives ax^2 >= 0.
Add q to both sides of ax^2 >= 0 to get ax^2 + q >= q, therefore f(x) >= q.
If a > 0, the range of f(x) = ax^2 + q is [q; infinity).
If a < 0, the range of f(x) = ax^2 + q is (-infinity; q].
For g(x) = x^2 + 2, the range is found by starting from x^2 >= 0 and adding 2 to both sides, giving x^2 + 2 >= 2, so g(x) >= 2.
The range can be read from the graph: for f(x) = x^2, from the graph y >= 0 for all values of x.
The turning point of f(x) = ax^2 + q is determined by examining the range of the function.
If a > 0, the graph of f(x) is a “smile” and has a minimum turning point at (0, q).
If a < 0, the graph of f(x) is a “frown” and has a maximum turning point at (0, q).
The axis of symmetry for functions of the form f(x) = ax^2 + q is the y-axis, which is the line x = 0.
For f(x) = x^2, as x increases from -infinity to 0, f(x) decreases.
For f(x) = x^2, as x increases from 0 to infinity, f(x) increases.
Every point on the y-axis has an x-coordinate of 0.
To calculate the y-intercept, let x = 0.
The y-intercept of g(x) = x^2 + 2 is found by setting x = 0, which gives g(0) = 0^2 + 2 = 2.
An intercept is written as a point with the coordinates separated by a semicolon, for example the y-intercept (0, 2).
Every point on the x-axis has a y-coordinate of 0.
To calculate the x-intercepts, let y = 0.
If setting y = 0 leaves an equation with no real solution (for g(x) = x^2 + 2 this gives -2 = x^2), the graph has no x-intercepts.
For g(x) = -1/2 x^2 - 3, setting y = 0 leads to -6 = x^2, which has no real solution, therefore there are no x-intercepts.
The graph of f(x) = x^2 intercepts the axes at the origin (0, 0).
To sketch a graph of the form f(x) = ax^2 + q, determine the sign of a, the y-intercept, the x-intercept(s) and the turning point.
To plot a parabola by points, substitute values of x into the equation to complete a table of values.
Plot the points from the table of values and join them with a smooth curve.
Examine the standard form of the equation: if a > 0, the graph is a “smile” and has a minimum turning point.
For the y-intercept, let x = 0; for y = 2x^2 - 4 this gives y = -4, the point (0, -4).
For the x-intercepts, let y = 0 and solve; for y = 2x^2 - 4 this gives x^2 = 2, so x = plus or minus the square root of 2.
The x-intercepts of y = 2x^2 - 4 are the points (-root 2; 0) and (root 2; 0).
Determine the turning point from the standard form of the equation; for y = 2x^2 - 4 the turning point is (0, -4).
Plot the intercepts and the turning point, then sketch the graph.
Examine the standard form of the equation: if a < 0, the graph is a “frown” and has a maximum turning point.
For g(x) = -1/2 x^2 - 3 the turning point is (0, -3), read from the standard form of the equation.
For g(x) = -1/2 x^2 - 3, the sketched graph has axis of symmetry the line x = 0.
To complete a table of values for h(x) = 1/x, substitute each given x-value into the equation and calculate h(x), for example h(-3) = 1/(-3) = -1/3.
For h(x) = 1/x, the value at x = 0 is 1/0, which is undefined.
To plot a hyperbola from the table, plot the points that the table gives and join them with two smooth curves.
For h(x) = 1/x, the function is undefined at x = 0; this is called a discontinuity at x = 0.
Since y = h(x) = 1/x, we can write x × y = 1.
The graph of h(x) = 1/x lies in the first and third quadrants, because the product of two positive numbers and the product of two negative numbers can both equal 1.
For h(x) = 1/x, as x gets larger, h(x) gets closer to, but does not equal, 0; this is a horizontal asymptote, the line y = 0.
In the third quadrant, as x gets smaller, h(x) also approaches the negative x-axis asymptotically.
For h(x) = 1/x there is a vertical asymptote, the line x = 0; as x gets closer to 0, h(x) approaches the y-axis asymptotically.
The graph of h(x) = 1/x has two axes of symmetry, the lines y = x and y = -x; about these two lines one half of the hyperbola is a mirror image of the other half.
Functions of the general form y = a/x + q are called hyperbolic functions.
To investigate the effect of q, plot y = 1/x - 2, y = 1/x - 1, y = 1/x, y = 1/x + 1 and y = 1/x + 2 on the same set of axes and use the results to deduce the effect of q.
To investigate the effect of a, plot y = -2/x, y = -1/x, y = 1/x and y = 2/x on the same set of axes and use the results to deduce the effect of a.
The effect of q is called a vertical shift, because all points are moved the same distance in the same direction (it slides the entire graph up or down).
For q > 0, the graph of f(x) is shifted vertically upwards by q units.
For q < 0, the graph of f(x) is shifted vertically downwards by q units.
The horizontal asymptote of y = a/x + q is the line y = q.
The vertical asymptote of y = a/x + q is always the y-axis, the line x = 0.
The sign of a determines the shape of the graph.
If a > 0, the graph of f(x) lies in the first and third quadrants.
For a > 1, the graph of f(x) will be further away from the axes than y = 1/x.
For 0 < a < 1, as a tends to 0, the graph moves closer to the axes than y = 1/x.
If a < 0, the graph of f(x) lies in the second and fourth quadrants.
For a < -1, the graph of f(x) will be further away from the axes than y = -1/x.
For -1 < a < 0, as a tends to 0, the graph moves closer to the axes than y = -1/x.
For y = a/x + q, the function is undefined for x = 0, so the domain is {x : x in R, x not equal to 0}.
To find the range of y = a/x + q, rewrite the equation to make x the subject: y - q = a/x, then (y - q)x = a for x not equal to 0, then x = a/(y - q).
The rewritten function is undefined only at y = q.
The range of y = a/x + q is {f(x) : f(x) in R, f(x) not equal to q}.
For h(x) = 1/x, the range read from the graph is {y : y in R, y not equal to 0}, since y is defined for all values except 0.
For g(x) = 2/x + 2, the domain is {x : x in R, x not equal to 0} because g(x) is undefined only at x = 0.
For g(x) = 2/x + 2, g(x) is undefined only at y = 2, so the range is {g(x) : g(x) in R, g(x) not equal to 2}.
To calculate the y-intercept, let x = 0, because every point on the y-axis has an x-coordinate of 0.
For g(x) = 2/x + 2, setting x = 0 gives 2/0 + 2, which is undefined, therefore there is no y-intercept.
To calculate the x-intercept, let y = 0, because every point on the x-axis has a y-coordinate of 0.
For g(x) = 2/x + 2, setting y = 0 gives 2/x = -2 and x = -1, so the x-intercept is the point (-1, 0).
There are two asymptotes for functions of the form y = a/x + q.
The horizontal asymptote is the line y = q and the vertical asymptote is always the y-axis, the line x = 0.
A hyperbola of the form y = a/x + q is symmetrical about two lines: y = x + q and y = -x + q.
To sketch a graph of the form y = f(x) = a/x + q, determine four characteristics: the sign of a, the y-intercept, the x-intercept and the asymptotes.
